prompt: Name TWO stains used when preparing a wet mount of cells for a light microscope, and state why a stain is used.
answer: Iodine solution and methylene blue (also acceptable: eosin). A stain is used because most cell structures are transparent, and the stain makes them visible by colouring them differently.
explanation: Iodine stains starch grains and plant cell walls; methylene blue is taken up by the nucleus of an animal cell. Without a stain the contrast between a structure and the cytoplasm around it is too low to see, however good the lens.

prompt: Name the TWO regions of a plant in which meristematic tissue is found, and state what meristematic cells do that mature cells do not.
answer: The apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots, and the lateral meristem (cambium) in the stem and root. Meristematic cells divide.
explanation: Meristem is the plant's only dividing tissue, which is why growth in a plant is confined to particular places rather than spread through the body as in an animal. Apical meristem lengthens the plant; the cambium thickens it.

prompt: Name the tissue that forms the outermost layer of a leaf, and name the pores in it through which gases enter and leave.
answer: The epidermis; the pores are stomata.
explanation: The upper epidermis is usually covered by a waxy cuticle that limits water loss, and most stomata are in the lower epidermis, where they are shaded and lose less water. Each stoma is opened and closed by a pair of guard cells.

prompt: Name THREE structures found in a typical plant cell that are absent from a typical animal cell.
answer: A cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central (permanent) vacuole.
explanation: Each corresponds to something plants do and animals do not: the cellulose wall provides support in an organism that has no skeleton, chloroplasts make food from light, and the large vacuole stores cell sap and holds the cell turgid against the wall.

prompt: Name the TWO transport tissues in a plant, and state what each one transports.
answer: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral salts; phloem transports manufactured food (sucrose and amino acids).
explanation: They also differ in direction and in whether they are alive. Xylem moves water upward only, in vessels whose cells are dead and hollow at maturity; phloem moves food in either direction, in living sieve tubes supported by companion cells.

prompt: Name the protein fibre that gives connective tissue its tensile strength, and name the cell that produces it.
answer: Collagen, produced by fibroblasts.
explanation: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body, and the amount and arrangement of it is what distinguishes one connective tissue from another: densely packed parallel collagen makes a tendon, and a loose irregular mesh of it makes areolar tissue.

prompt: Name the building block (monomer) of a protein, and name the bond that joins two of them together.
answer: The amino acid; joined by a peptide bond.
explanation: Twenty different amino acids, joined in different orders, give every protein a unique sequence. That sequence is the primary structure, and because it determines how the chain folds, it determines the shape of the protein and therefore what it can do.

prompt: Name THREE structures found in a bacterial cell, and state the term used for a cell that has no true nucleus.
answer: Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA (nucleoid), plasmid, capsule, flagellum (any three). Such a cell is prokaryotic.
explanation: Prokaryotic means before a nucleus: the DNA lies free in the cytoplasm rather than enclosed in a nuclear membrane. Prokaryotes also lack mitochondria, chloroplasts and every other membrane-bound organelle, which is the deeper division in biology.

prompt: Name the THREE types of muscle tissue found in the human body.
answer: Skeletal (striated) muscle, smooth (involuntary) muscle and cardiac muscle.
explanation: They differ in where they are, whether they can be controlled at will, and how they tire. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and fatigues; smooth muscle in the gut and blood vessels is involuntary and slow; cardiac muscle is involuntary and does not fatigue at all.

prompt: State ONE location of skeletal muscle and ONE location of cardiac muscle in the body, and state which of the two is under voluntary control.
answer: Skeletal muscle is attached to the bones of the limbs (for example the biceps); cardiac muscle is found only in the wall of the heart. Skeletal muscle is voluntary.
explanation: Cardiac muscle is unique in being able to contract rhythmically without any nervous signal, because its cells generate their own impulse and are joined by intercalated discs that pass it from cell to cell. That is why a heart continues to beat when its nerve supply is cut.

prompt: Name the protein in a red blood cell that carries oxygen, name the mineral it contains, and state which organelle a mature red blood cell lacks.
answer: Haemoglobin; it contains iron; a mature red blood cell has no nucleus.
explanation: Losing the nucleus frees space for more haemoglobin and lets the cell take a biconcave shape with a larger surface area, but it also means the cell cannot repair itself or divide, which is why red blood cells survive only about 120 days.

prompt: Name the cell that makes up nervous tissue, and name the part of it that carries an impulse AWAY from the cell body.
answer: The neuron (nerve cell); the axon carries impulses away from the cell body.
explanation: Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body and the axon carries them away, so the direction of travel through a neuron is fixed by its structure. A single axon may be more than a metre long, which is how one cell can span from the spinal cord to the foot.

prompt: Name the meristem responsible for an increase in the LENGTH of a plant, and the meristem responsible for an increase in its GIRTH.
answer: The apical meristem lengthens the plant; the lateral meristem (cambium) increases its girth.
explanation: This is why a nail driven into a tree trunk stays at the same height for the life of the tree: growth in length happens only at the tips, so the trunk below a growing point is mature tissue that does not stretch. The cambium simply grows around the nail.

prompt: Name the FOUR basic types of tissue found in animals.
answer: Epithelial tissue, connective tissue, muscle tissue and nervous tissue.
explanation: Every organ in an animal body is built from some combination of these four. The stomach, for example, has an epithelial lining, connective tissue beneath it, layers of smooth muscle to churn its contents, and nervous tissue coordinating the whole.

prompt: State the general function of epithelial tissue, and name ONE place in the body where it is found.
answer: It covers body surfaces and lines cavities, tubes and organs, forming a protective boundary. It is found in the skin, the lining of the gut, the trachea, the kidney tubules or the alveoli.
explanation: Because it forms the boundary, everything entering or leaving the body crosses an epithelium, which is why its thickness varies so much with its job: a single flat layer at an alveolus where diffusion must be fast, and many layers in skin where abrasion must be resisted.

prompt: State what a tendon joins, and state what a ligament joins.
answer: A tendon joins muscle to bone. A ligament joins bone to bone.
explanation: Their jobs explain their different make-up. A tendon must transmit a pull without stretching, so its collagen fibres are packed in parallel; a ligament must hold a joint together while allowing movement, so it contains elastic fibres as well and can stretch a little.

prompt: Name the cell that produces cartilage, and name TWO places in the human body where cartilage is found.
answer: The chondrocyte (chondroblast). Cartilage is found at the ends of long bones, in the nose and ear, in the trachea, between the vertebrae and at the ribs' attachment to the sternum (any two).
explanation: Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own, so chondrocytes are supplied only by diffusion through the matrix. That is why cartilage grows and repairs very slowly, and why a torn knee cartilage is a far more serious injury than a broken bone.

prompt: State the number of cell layers in a SIMPLE epithelium, and state the number in a STRATIFIED epithelium.
answer: A simple epithelium is one cell layer thick; a stratified epithelium is more than one cell layer thick.
explanation: The number of layers follows the job. Simple epithelium is found where substances must cross quickly, as at an alveolus or a kidney tubule; stratified epithelium is found where the surface is worn away and must be replaced, as in skin and the mouth.

prompt: Name the FOUR phases of mitosis, in the order in which they occur.
answer: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
explanation: Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms in prophase, chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, chromatids are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase, and two new nuclei form in telophase. Interphase, the long growth and DNA-replication stage, comes before all of them and is not part of mitosis.

prompt: Name the tissue that transports water in a plant, state the direction in which that water moves, and name the process that drives the movement.
answer: Xylem; water moves upward, from root to leaf; the movement is driven by transpiration (the transpiration pull).
explanation: Water evaporating from the leaves lowers the pressure at the top of the xylem, and because water molecules cling to one another by cohesion, the whole column is drawn up as one. No energy is spent by the plant, which is how water reaches the top of a very tall tree.

prompt: Name the THREE main parts of a neuron.
answer: The cell body, the dendrites and the axon.
explanation: The cell body holds the nucleus and does the cell's housekeeping; the dendrites are short branches that receive impulses from other neurons; and the axon is the single long fibre that carries the impulse away, often wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath that speeds transmission.

prompt: State the number of daughter cells produced by one mitotic division, and state how their chromosome number compares with that of the parent cell.
answer: Two daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
explanation: Mitosis is a copying process, not a halving one: the DNA is replicated during interphase and then divided equally, so each daughter cell receives a full and identical set. That is what makes mitosis suitable for growth, repair and asexual reproduction, and unsuitable for making gametes.

prompt: State TWO differences between a monocotyledonous plant and a dicotyledonous plant.
answer: Any two of: one seed leaf against two; parallel leaf venation against net venation; scattered vascular bundles in the stem against bundles in a ring; fibrous roots against a tap root; flower parts in threes against fours or fives.
explanation: These features travel together because they reflect two early branches of the flowering plants. The grouping is practical as well as evolutionary: maize, wheat and grasses are monocots, while beans, sunflowers and most broad-leaved trees are dicots.

prompt: Name the type of muscle tissue found in the wall of the heart, and state whether it is under voluntary or involuntary control.
answer: Cardiac muscle; it is involuntary.
explanation: Cardiac muscle is found nowhere else in the body. Its cells branch and are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which lets an impulse spread through the whole wall at once so that the chambers contract as a unit rather than fibre by fibre.

prompt: Name the tissue that transports manufactured food in a plant, name the living cells through which that food moves, and name the process.
answer: Phloem; the food moves through sieve tube cells; the process is translocation.
explanation: Unlike xylem, phloem is alive and can move food in either direction — up to a growing shoot in spring, down to the roots in autumn. Each sieve tube cell is kept working by an adjacent companion cell, which supplies the ATP that translocation requires.

prompt: State TWO features of skeletal muscle tissue that can be seen under a light microscope.
answer: Any two of: light and dark cross-striations; long cylindrical fibres; many nuclei per fibre, positioned at the edge of the fibre; unbranched fibres lying parallel.
explanation: The striations are the regular overlap of actin and myosin filaments, which is the arrangement that produces contraction. The many nuclei come from many cells fusing during development, so a single muscle fibre is not a single cell.

prompt: State the function of nervous tissue.
answer: To receive stimuli and to transmit impulses rapidly from one part of the body to another, coordinating the body's responses.
explanation: Speed is what distinguishes it from the body's other coordinating system. Hormones travel in the blood and act over minutes to days; a nerve impulse travels along a myelinated axon at up to about 120 m·s⁻¹, which is what makes a reflex possible.
